analysis.one_liner: Caps consumer credit interest rates at 15 percent nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap credit card interest rates at 15 percent never got a committee vote in the Senate Banking Committee; no action after referral.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee never took it up after referral; Congress ended 2011-01-03.

narrative.text: Introduced March 12, 2009 and referred to Banking.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers and banks kept charging rates above 15%; borrowers paid more.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap consumer APRs at 15 percent.

for.name: Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Joined Sanders in introducing the bill.

against.name: Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee never scheduled action on the bill after referral.

against.name: Banking and credit card industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed national interest rate caps, arguing they would restrict credit availability.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was an Independent with 7 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support; the Banking Committee, chaired by a Democrat, took no action.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: A 15 percent national APR cap would directly limit the rates and fees they could charge on credit card balances.
The bill exempts credit unions from the cap, leaving them free to set rates while bank competitors are capped.
A 15 percent cap would end their business model of charging triple-digit APRs on small loans.
